chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ibn Abi Najran, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) regarding His words
He said: 'It means the grasping of the imagination. Do you not see His words:
'There has come to you Insight from your Lord' [6:104]

It does not mean the sight of the eyes. 'Whoever therefore sees, it is for his own soul' — it does not mean seeing with his physical eye. 'And whoever is blind, it shall be against himself' — it does not mean the blindness of the eyes. Rather, He meant the grasping of the imagination,

just as it is said: so and so has insight in poetry, and so and so has insight in jurisprudence, and so and so has insight in Dirhams, and so and so has insight in clothes. God is more magnificent than that He should be seen with the eye.'

key_terms.إحاطة الوهم: Grasping of the imagination/intellect — the cognitive faculty that attempts to encompass God
key_terms.الأبصار: Visions/sights — plural of basar, here interpreted as the comprehending capacity of imagination, not physical eyesight
key_terms.بصائر: Insights/clear proofs — intellectual perspicacity, contrasted with physical sight

ai.seo_question: Can God be seen with physical eyes according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) explains that the Quranic phrase 'visions cannot comprehend Him' (6:103) does not refer to physical sight but to the grasping capacity of the human imagination and intellect. He substantiates this with the immediately following verse (6:104), where 'insight' (basar) clearly refers to intellectual understanding, not physical vision — just as Arabic usage speaks of someone having 'insight' in poetry, law, or commerce. This is a fundamental Shia theological argument against the belief that God can be seen with physical eyes (ru'yat Allah), affirming divine transcendence.
word_analysis: it is for his own soul
